turns.text: The previous story examined Bagging. Now the camera turns to Random Forests and a new question along the same timeline: Turn the clock back to 2001. What problem was Random Forests actually trying to solve?
Bagging reduced tree variance, but strongly correlated trees still made similar errors. Random forests introduced additional randomness at each split so the ensemble would contain stronger diversity.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?
Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample and considers only a random subset of features at each node. Voting or averaging many decorrelated trees yields strong accuracy with little tuning.
Why did the idea outlive one paper or experiment? What did later researchers actually inherit?

Experts generally regard random forests as one of the most durable general-purpose machine-learning methods. They remain competitive on structured data and provide useful tools for feature importance, proximity, and uncertainty analysis.
Random Forests mattered not only as a result, but as a method that later researchers could test, adapt, and extend.
